title: Antibody waning and Bordetella pertussis resurgence after the COVID-19 pandemic in the Netherlands

paper_content.abstract: After relative absence of Bordetella pertussis during the COVID-19 pandemic, notifications in the Netherlands were increased from May 2023 till September 2024. We monitored the largest pertussis outbreak in decades and investigated underlying immunological dynamics based on IgG and IgA antibodies against pertussis antigens (Ptx, FHA & Prn). We analyzed serum from 418 participants (2–87 years) at five time points (November 2022-October 2024) from a nationwide prospective serosurveillance study (PIENTER-Corona). Weighted incidence over two years was 6.3% (95% CI: 4.4-8.2) in the Dutch population, and 35% (95% CI: 26.2-44.6) in 6-18 y-olds. Children aged 6-12 years, who received a booster vaccination at 4 years, showed lowest anti-Ptx IgG concentrations after the period of reduced circulation. Infected individuals had lower pre-infection anti-FHA IgG and IgA concentrations than matched uninfected individuals. Prolonged coughing was reported by 16% of the infected individuals. Our findings highlight the B. pertussis outbreak was preceded by waning immunity, particularly after acellular pertussis booster vaccination. The small proportion of symptomatic infections implies sufficient protection by the vaccine against disease but not transmission.
paper_content.introduction:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), including wearing face masks, social distancing, closure of schools and working from home, were introduced to limit the circulation of SARS-CoV-2. This not only led to a reduction of SARS-CoV-2 notifications but also to a decrease of notifications of other airborne-transmissible pathogens, including pertussis, or whooping cough, a disease caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis (Fig. 1)1–3. Notably, this reduction of pertussis notifications likely reflects reduced circulation of the bacterium, which lasted for almost 3 years. Since May 2023, pertussis notifications rose, cumulating in the largest pertussis outbreak to date since 2012 in the Netherlands (Fig. 1)2. This trend has been observed in multiple Europe countries2,3.

Pertussis is a highly contagious respiratory infection. During the catarrhal stage, symptoms mostly resemble those of a common cold. In the paroxysmal phase, which is the most symptomatic stage, symptoms are often coughing, inspiratory whooping and post-tussive vomiting4. Infections can occur at any age but can cause serious disease in (predominantly unvaccinated) infants and older adults4. Vaccinated individuals are more likely to have an atypical, mild, or even asymptomatic infection5. Since the use of the whole cell pertussis (wP) vaccine—containing inactivated bacteria—in the Dutch national immunization program (NIP) in 1957, a drop in the incidence of pertussis was recorded6. Despite vaccination, re-emergence was apparent as of 1996, with incidence peaking every 3–5 years7. In 2001, an acellular pertussis (aP) booster vaccination, containing inactivated pertussis toxin (Ptx), filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA), pertactin (Prn) and sometimes fimbriae 2/3 (Fim 2/3), was implemented at 4 years of age2. In 2005, the wP vaccine for the primary series was also replaced by an aP vaccine due to high reactogenicity of the wP vaccine2. Despite these changes, pertussis incidence remained high and a threat for infants too young to be vaccinated2. Of special concern is the decrease in vaccination coverage in the Netherlands that has been observed over the past years. The WHO and RIVM reported that the percentage of fully vaccinated infants by the age of two declined from 96 to 97% in the 2010 birth cohort to 92–94% in the 2019 birth cohort and 89–93% in the 2022 birth cohort8,9. Since 2019, the maternal diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccination is implemented in the Dutch NIP to increase the level of maternally-derived immunological protection in the first months post birth2. However, this is not implemented globally, and pertussis remains one of the least controlled vaccine-preventable diseases.

As B. pertussis generally circulates continuously, leading to notifications year-round, there is no clear understanding of what drives the epidemiology and the elevation of notifications every 3–5 years. Notably, while respiratory syncytial virus and seasonal coronaviruses re-appeared rapidly when most NPIs for COVID-19 were lifted mid-2022, pertussis notifications increased nearly a year later (Fig. 1). The period of reduced B. pertussis circulation provided a unique opportunity to monitor waning immunity against B. pertussis and how changes in immunity may have affected the rapid increase of notifications from 2023 onwards. We use a Dutch nationwide prospective cohort (2–87 year of age), setup since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, to investigate the age-specific incidence of B. pertussis infections between November 2022 and October 2024. We identify an overall 6.4% incidence, and an incidence of 35.4% in children aged 6–18 years during this two-year period, which is caused by the combined effect of waning vaccine immunity and a prolonged period of reduced pertussis circulation.
paper_content.results:
Study population
The participants for this study were part of the PICO cohort and resided across the country (Supplementary Fig. 1A). Slightly more women were included compared to men (Table 1). Vaccination coverage in children based on long-term protection anti-Ttx IgG (>0.1 IU/ml) was estimated to be 98.9% at baseline (i.e., November 2022). Overall, anti-Ttx IgG antibodies were detected in 95.2% of the included participants.

Overall anti-Ptx IgG concentrations by age were determined at the start and end of the study (Fig. 2A). At the start, lower concentrations were observed in 6–12-year-old individuals as compared to 2–5-year-olds and adults (p < 0.005). Anti-Ptx IgG concentrations of 6–12-year-old individuals had increased in October 2024 as compared to those at the start of the study (p < 0.001), despite large variation (Fig. 2B). In all other age groups, no significantly different concentrations were observed between both sampling rounds (Fig. 2B).

Pertussis infections during the study period
Antibody rises attributed to DTaP or Tdap vaccination during the study period were observed in the 2–5 years age group (13 cases) and in the 19–39 years age group (4 cases) (Fig. 3A, blue lines). The weighted incidence of B. pertussis infections in the general Dutch population—based on the serological criteria in the current study—was 0.6% between November 2022 and April 2023, 1.4% between April and November 2023, 3.5% between November 2023 and April 2024, and 1.5% between April and October 2024 (Table 1 and Fig. 3A, orange lines). The weighted cumulative incidence in the Dutch population (2–87 years) during this two-year period was estimated at 6.3%. The highest incidence (35.4%) was found among the age group 6–18 years (Fig. 3B and Table 1). The increase in anti-Ptx IgG concentrations after infection was also paralleled by an increase in anti-FHA and anti-Prn IgG and IgA and anti-Ptx IgA concentrations (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Individuals with serological evidence of B. pertussis infection did not report increased symptoms compared to uninfected individuals. Prolonged coughing (>2 weeks) during the past year was reported by 16% of the infected individuals between 6 and 18 years (5/32) in the last sampling round, of whom two contacted the GP. No significant difference was observed concerning prolonged coughing in uninfected individuals (22/75 (29.3%); p = 0.21).

Because the higher pertussis incidence according to serological detections, including age group differences (Table 1), and the syndromic notifications (Supplementary Fig. 1B), the serological infection prevalence based on anti-Ptx IgG categories was further estimated in an additional subset in October 2024. The additional cross-sectional subset showed a similar proportion of individuals with no indication of recent infection (<50 IU/mL) in the 6–18, 19–39, and 60+ year age groups compared to the longitudinal cohort (Supplementary Fig. 4). The 40–59 years age group indicated a lower proportion of recently infected individuals in the longitudinal serosurvey in October 2024 compared to the cross-sectional study (p = 0.0028) (Supplementary Fig. 4).

The cross-sectional subset from October 2024 was also compared with previous cross-sectional serosurveys conducted using similar methodologies7. All age groups show a similar proportion of individuals with no indication of recent infection compared to the Pienter-2 study (2006–2007) and the Pienter-3 study (2016–2017) except for individuals in the 40–59 years age group (Fig. 4). The additional subset from October 2024 showed a higher proportion of individuals without indication of recent infection compared to the Pienter-3 study (p = 0.045).

Antibody waning
To address whether the lower anti-Ptx IgG concentrations within the 6–18 years age group in November 2022 (Fig. 2) might be related to a more rapid antibody waning after (primary series or booster) vaccination, a linear mixed-effects model was applied in individuals who remained uninfected or up the point of infection and unvaccinated. The 2–5 year-olds showed the highest anti-Ptx IgG concentrations at the start of the study (16.45 IU/mL; p < 0.05 compared to other age groups). The 6–12 years age group displayed lower antibody concentrations at the start of the study period compared to adults (5.83 IU/mL vs. 7.28 IU/mL; p = 0.009). The fastest antibody decay was observed in the 2–5 years age group with the duration of antibody decay to 50% of 17.8 months (Fig. 5; p < 0.001 for the slope). Antibody decay was also noticed in the 6–12, 13–18 and ≥19 years age group (p < 0.001 for the slopes). The duration of antibody decay to 50% in the 6–12, 13–18, and ≥19 years age group was 48.5, 102.5 and 84.1 months, respectively.

Anti-Ptx, FHA and Prn concentrations in individuals 6–18 years
Anti-FHA IgG concentrations of infected individuals between 6 and 18 years of age appeared significantly lower prior to infection compared to age-matched uninfected individuals (13.4 IU/mL (95% CI 9.8–18.2) vs. 27.9 IU/mL (95% CI 22.1–35.1); p = 0.002), as well as anti-FHA IgA concentrations (1.0 IU/mL (95% CI 0.8–1.4) vs. 2.1 IU/mL (95% CI 1.6-2.8); p = 0.006) (Fig. 6B, E). Comparison of anti-Ptx, anti-Prn IgG, and IgA concentrations revealed no statistically significant differences, nor did the control antigen rubella IgG concentrations.

Using the Youden index, protective cut-off values for anti-FHA IgG and IgA were estimated. This resulted in cutoffs of 13.6 and 1.6 IU/mL for IgG and IgA respectively, with corresponding AUC values of 0.74 and 0.72 (specificity of 78% and 63% and sensitivity of 71% and 74%, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 5). We found no conclusive evidence that individuals who reporting (prolonged) cough symptoms had statistically significant lower anti-Ptx IgG and IgA concentrations, although the numbers were low (p = 0.084 and p = 0.051, respectively).
paper_content.methods:
Study population
The PIENTER-corona (PICO) study was setup at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic to study immunity to SARS-CoV-2 across the Dutch population with repeated sampling of the same individuals (~10,000 unique participants) until the end of 2024 (in total 13 study rounds), as described previously37,40,41. The PICO-study protocol was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee MEC-U, the Netherlands (Clinical Trial Registration NTR8473), and conformed to the principles embodied in the Declaration of Helsinki. Informed consent was obtained from all adult participants and from parents or legal guardians of minors prior to participation.

Here, we randomly selected an age-stratified subset with completed questionnaires and samples (n = 419) from study rounds 9–13 (November 2022–October 2024) (age range: 2–87 years). Because of the vaccination schedule and expected incidence in children, smaller age windows were used (Table 1). For the overall analysis, we expected a 6% incidence rate7 and aimed for a one-sided precision of 2.5%, resulting in a minimum required sample size of 347 individuals (α = 0.05, power = 80%). Taking into account a potential loss of 15% of follow-up samples, at least 408 participants were needed in the longitudinal analysis. For all age groups, we were able to include sufficient individuals, except for the youngest age group (2–5 years), where only 43 individuals were available, who were all included.

To investigate changes in antibody concentrations, samples were collected in November 2022 (median inclusion date: 8 November), April 2023 (median: 25 April), and November 2023 (median: 6 November) (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Sampling volumes were adequate for all but one participant, and serum samples from one participant had to be excluded due to technical issues, so serum samples from 418 participants could be tested. Since the pertussis notifications were still elevated after November 2023, follow-up samples collected in April 2024 (median: 15 April; 382 participants (91%)) and October 2024 (median: 14 October; 358 participants (85%)) were included as well.

Participants sent in a fingerstick blood sample in a microtainer by mail. Serum obtained from these blood samples was stored at −20°C awaiting analyses. The participants completed a questionnaire during each sampling round, including, amongst others, questions about sociodemographic characteristics, COVID-19-related symptoms (general, respiratory, and gastrointestinal) in the past months and behavioral factors. Each round, participants were requested to report respiratory symptoms, including cough, sore throat and runny nose and fever, which are associated with B. pertussis infection24. In the final sampling round, a specific question about prolonged coughing (>2 weeks) in the past year was added.

Detection of antibodies
Serum samples were tested for anti-Ptx, anti-tetanus toxin (Ttx; to control for vaccination) and anti-rubella (as an independent control to monitor antibody variation) IgG antibodies at all sampling rounds using an in-house validated fluorescent bead-based multiplex immunoassay as described before42,43. During the last three sampling rounds, most infections were detected, hence, these samples were tested additionally for anti-FHA and anti-Prn IgG and IgA and Ptx IgA (see Supplementary Methods for further details on the assay).

Criteria for pertussis infection
Active or recent infection with B. pertussis was detected by an increase in Ptx-specific antibodies44. Diagnostic confirmation of recent pertussis infection in paired samples, with the second sample at 2–4 weeks interval, normally uses a >3-fold increase in anti-Ptx IgG concentration with a final concentration >20 IU/mL44–46. Here, we used a ≥2-fold increase criterion due to a longer time interval between two measurements. We expected more waning of antibodies within that period, consequently leading to a lower fold-change between consecutive samples. For participants of whom a sample was missing in November 2022 (n = 1) or April 2024 (n = 11), an infection could be ruled out as they remained below the cutoff in the subsequent round (April 2023 or October 2024).

Part of the participants in this study could have elevated anti-Ptx concentrations due to DTaP or Tdap infant, booster or maternal vaccination (Table 2). For children <5 years of age and women who reported to be pregnant, a ≥2-fold increase in anti-Ptx IgG and anti-Ttx IgG concentrations with anti-Ptx IgG concentrations >5 IU/mL indicated a recent (maternal) vaccination. Because the Tdap booster vaccination contains reduced concentrations of the pertussis components, and vaccination induces a weaker antibody response compared to natural infection, a lower anti-Ptx IgG cutoff was used not to miss vaccination events47. The validity of this approach was tested on sera from individuals seeking medical care with confirmed pertussis infection (see Supplementary Methods).

In addition, a (cross-sectional) estimation of infection prevalence was conducted with an additional sample from the last PICO round (October 2024, n = 761) and compared with the longitudinal data from November 2022 and October 2024 and two cross-sectional serosurveys that were carried out in the past using the same measurements (Pienter-2, 2006/2007 and Pienter-3, 2016/2017)7,48. As the earlier surveys did not include sequential sampling, the definition used in our analysis so far could not be used for this comparison. As applied previously, we used anti-Ptx IgG concentrations of ≥100 IU/mL as the most stringent diagnostic criterium associated with a recent infection in the past 6 months44, concentrations between 50 and 100 IU/mL for an infection in the past 6–12 months, and those under 50 IU/mL for a less recent infection7,49.

Statistical analyses
Data cleaning and statistical analyses were performed using Rstudio (R version 4.4.0, R Core Team, Vienna, Austria) using packages nlme50, MatchIt51, effects52 and pROC53 and SAS v.9.4. (SAS Institute Inc., USA). For all analyses, age at the moment of inclusion (November 2022) was used, unless specified otherwise. The antibody data were log-transformed, and Loess (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing) curves were generated to visualize antibody concentrations across all ages at the start and end point of the study. A two-sided paired t-test on log-transformed data was used to compare the anti-Ptx IgG concentrations at the start and end point of the study for different age groups. An two-sided unpaired t-test on log-transformed data was used to compare the anti-Ptx IgG concentrations at the start of the study period between age groups.

Pertussis incidence per study round, cumulative incidence across the study period and seroprevalence estimated (with 95% confidence intervals (CI)) were calculated taking into account the survey design (with regions as strata and municipalities as clusters, where applicable), and weighted on age, sex, ethnic background and degree of urbanization following census data from the statistics Netherlands of the respected periods to match the general Dutch population, as described previously40. Estimates were provided for the overall population and by age group. For the pertussis incidence per study round, age during the specific round was used. Differences in seroprevalence between groups were assessed by estimating the parameters of the beta distribution using the method of moments. Risk ratios and their 95% Cis and two-sided p-values were calculated based on Monte Carlo simulations, and reported where applicable.

Waning of anti-Ptx IgG concentrations per age group was evaluated in individuals who remained uninfected (or up the point of infection) and unvaccinated with a linear mixed-effects model on log-transformed values, using the nlme package. The model contained random intercepts and slopes per age group, and the fixed effect was constructed as the interaction of time and age. The results are expressed as the predicted geometric mean concentrations of anti-Ptx IgG per age group and PICO study round with corresponding 95% CIs.

Pre-infection IgG and IgA antibody concentrations against B. pertussis antigens implicated in host colonization (FHA and Prn) were compared between participants with a confirmed infection (n = 38) and uninfected controls (n = 68) matched by age and sampling round. Antibodies to the independent antigen rubella served as control to monitor antibody variations. Log-transformed IgG concentrations were compared with a t-test and IgA concentrations with a Mann–Whitney U test due to not normally distributed data. Finally, to approximate the sensitivity and specificity of a potential correlate of protection, the Youden index of the receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curve analysis were used.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Outbreaks of pertussis are observed in many countries after the COVID-19 pandemic. In Europe, the highest incidence is reported in adolescents aged 10 to 19 years. Although multiple reasons are proposed to explain the outbreaks, the exact mechanisms are not known. This study included serum samples collected from 418 participants aged 2 to 87 years at five time points (November 2022-October 2024) of a nationwide prospective serosurveillance study conducted in the Netherlands and analyzed the concentrations of anti-PT IgG antibodies. They found that cumulative infection incidence was 6.3% in the Dutch population, and 35% in 6-18y-olds. The study provided an important information why the incidence of pertussis was high in adolescents during the outbreaks after the pandemic. The study design is proper and the finding is novel. I have following concerns which should be addressed first.
1. A table to describe the current vaccination program of pertussis is needed, this will help understand the waning vaccine-induced immunity.
2. The PICO study included about 10,000 participants. However, only 419 were randomly selected for the study. What is the statistical justification for the selection? Based on the early European seroprevalence studies (Wehlin et al APIMS 2021 and Berbers et al 2021), the sample size is estimated to be 250 samples/age group of 10 years e.g. 250 samples in age group of 20-29 years old.
This is especially important issue since the study failed to identify the cases with recent infections in age groups older than 19 years.
3. The finding that participants of 6 to 18 years had low FHA IgG concentrations prior to infection was interesting. This finding was consistent with an early study conducted in Finland (He et al, JID 1994) in which they showed schoolchildren with high FHA IgG antibodies are protected during outbreaks.
4. Another issue which should be discussed is that the FHA IgG antibodies can be induced by other Bordetella species or bacteria other than Bordetella.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors describe immunity of pertussis during COVID-19 focusing on periods of low and high activity. The paper is flawed by the inability to distinguish between infection vs vaccine induced antibodies and using rather arbitrary cut offs for immunity against tetanus (>5 units) and categorization of infection against pertussis (lines 112-115). The authors should have used a consistent definition for both pertussis and tetanus (e.g. 2 or more fold change , 4 or more fold change).
More detailed feedback and comments.
The manuscript addresses an important and timely issue: the resurgence of Bordetella pertussis in the post–COVID-19 era. Pertussis remains the least controlled vaccine-preventable disease, and its re-emergence is a global concern. Countries that transitioned from whole-cell (wP) to acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines have consistently reported shorter-lived immunity, increased susceptibility in adolescents and adults, and recurrent epidemics every 3–5 years. The COVID-19 pandemic, with its widespread non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), provided an unusual natural experiment by temporarily interrupting pathogen circulation. This interruption raised concerns that reduced natural immune boosting, combined with the already known rapid waning of aP-induced immunity, could exacerbate pertussis resurgence once restrictions were lifted. The manuscript correctly identifies this epidemiological and immunological interplay as the central concerns.
The authors address this issue by leveraging a nationwide prospective serosurveillance cohort to monitor antibody dynamics and infection incidence across age groups. Their data provide evidence that waning population immunity left certain groups (notably children and adolescents) more susceptible, which contributed to the sharp increase in cases from 2023 onwards. However, while the cohort design is robust and the longitudinal sampling a strength, the study is limited in its ability to fully disentangle the interplay between vaccination history, natural boosting, and other epidemiological drivers (e.g., bacterial adaptation, changes in diagnostic practices, or underdiagnosis).
Another limitation is the heavy reliance on serological markers (IgG, IgA against Ptx, FHA, and Prn) as analogs of immunity or to propose protection surrogates. While informative, antibody concentrations alone may not fully capture protective immunity, especially given the growing recognition of the role of cellular responses in pertussis control. The authors acknowledge waning immunity but could have more critically contextualized their findings within the broader debate over the adequacy of current pertussis vaccination strategies.
In summary, the manuscript provides valuable national data on pertussis resurgence after the COVID-19 pandemic and highlights waning vaccine-induced immunity as a major driver. Yet, its framing could be strengthened by situating the findings within the broader global context of pertussis resurgence, addressing alternative explanations beyond antibody waning, and more explicitly discussing implications for vaccination policy.
Suggested corrections
Major
1. From line 39, the authors state that pertussis is often accompanied by whooping cough, but this is characteristic of the paroxysmal stage. In the catarrhal phase, symptoms are nonspecific and resemble those of a common cold. To avoid misinterpretation, the reviewer suggests deleting the second sentence of this paragraph and instead clarifying that during the paroxysmal phase—the most severe and symptomatic stage—patients experience episodes of spasmodic coughing fits, inspiratory whooping, and post-tussive vomiting.
2. The authors repeatedly refer to the use of tetanus toxin in their experiments. However, due to biosafety constraints, toxoids are more commonly used in these contexts. Could the authors clarify whether the toxic or atoxic form of the protein was employed?
3. While the Dutch National Immunization Programme (NIP) is publicly available, the reviewer recommends briefly outlining it in the introduction to aid reader understanding. To my understanding, pertussis acellular components are currently included in the hexavalent vaccine administered at 2/3, 5, and 12 months of age, with a booster at 5 years (trivalent vaccine). No further boosters are given, except in pregnant women to protect newborns early in life.
4. It is unclear why the anti-rubella response was used to assess vaccination history, since rubella vaccination is given separately and not concomitantly with pertussis or tetanus toxoid. In the Netherlands, MMR is administered at 14 months and 3 years of age, which differs from the pertussis vaccination schedule. If the aim was to assess recent pertussis vaccination, a non-vaccine pertussis antigen such as adenylate cyclase toxin might have been more appropriate. Could the authors explain the rationale behind selecting anti-rubella antibodies as a control? This is insufficiently clarified in the text and would benefit from further explanation.
5. In Figure 6, the authors should visually separate the anti-pertussis proteins results from those of anti-rubella antigens. The reviewer recommends adding a vertical, thick dotted or dashed line running top-to-bottom after panels C and F.
6. Although the manuscript mentions that wP vaccination (and natural infection) primarily induces Th1/Th17 responses—contrasting with the Th2 bias of aP vaccines—the authors did not examine the IgG1/IgG2 ratio in sera from convalescent, recently immunized, and low-titer individuals. This omission is a limitation, since IgG2 is suboptimal for opsonization and phagocytosis, and absolute quantification of aP-induced antibodies may overlook this. This point should be discussed in the manuscript. Moreover, recent studies suggest that aP vaccines generate antigen-specific regulatory T cells that compromise the induction of long-term mucosal immunity in the respiratory tract.
7. Line 358: Please clarify what the rubella material supplied by GenWay comprises. Is it a surface antigen or an inactivated virus?

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):

(lines 112-115). The authors should have used a consistent definition for both pertussis and tetanus (e.g. 2 or more

Response:
The reviewer raises two important issues: the discrimination between infection and vaccine-induced
antibodies, and the use of cutoffs.
The first issue of discriminating between infection and vaccine-induced antibodies is fundamental to our
studies, where we aimed to identify infections and not erroneously classify vaccination events as infections.
Here we disagree with the statement made by the reviewer that we cannot distinguish between infection and
vaccine-induced antibodies, as we paid close attention to, as accurately as possible, classify individuals with
increased anti-PT IgG concentrations as being recently infected. Indeed, the detection of antibodies to
pertussis itself cannot discriminate between infection and vaccination. This is why we added a validated
antibody assay for tetanus toxin to reliably detect instances of vaccination as this is part of the pertussis
vaccine as well which is a correct approach. We do realize however, that no laboratory test is 100% accurate
and that still some misclassification can occur. This we acknowledge in the Discussion of our manuscript lines
389-391.
Different cut-offs were applied for longitudinal respectively cross-sectional data analyses because this results in
more accurate (specificity and sensitivity) identification of infections. By doing so, we could benefit from the
longitudinal sampling to identify infections during the study period (a ≥2-fold increase together with a final
concentrations of ≥20 IU/mL). Whilst fold-changes is a sensitive method to identify infections, this is less
accurate at low concentrations due to more background variation, which is why we applied a concentration-
based cutoff to avoid cases being falsely classified as infections (20 IU/mL for anti-Ptx IgG). As the antibody
response to vaccination is weaker compared to infection, we decreased the cut-off for anti-Ptx-IgG from 20
IU/mL to 5 IU/mL. This lower cut-off revealed four additional vaccinated individuals who otherwise would have
been missed. To clarify why we used a different cut-off in longitudinal samples, we changed the following
sentence to the methods section:
Line 122-125: Because the Tdap booster vaccination contains reduced concentrations of the pertussis components, and
vaccination induces a weaker antibody response compared to natural infection, a lower anti-Ptx IgG cutoff was used to not
miss vaccination events.
For the additional cross-sectional sampling, we could only apply absolute levels indicative for recent infection
to allow comparison between studies (<50 IU/mL, 50-100 IU/mL and ≥100 IU/mL). The cut-off of 100 IU/mL is
also used in the diagnostic lab as cut-off for recent infection, while the 50-100 IU/mL cutoff is used by multiple
studies (1, 8).
These different analyses have been described separately in our Methods section and these cutoffs have been
applied consistently (lines 112-126).
More detailed feedback and comments.
The manuscript addresses an important and timely issue: the resurgence of Bordetella pertussis in the post–
COVID-19 era. Pertussis remains the least controlled vaccine-preventable disease, and its re-emergence is a
global concern. Countries that transitioned from whole-cell (wP) to acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines have
consistently reported shorter-lived immunity, increased susceptibility in adolescents and adults, and recurrent
epidemics every 3–5 years. The COVID-19 pandemic, with its widespread non-pharmaceutical interventions
(NPIs), provided an unusual natural experiment by temporarily interrupting pathogen circulation. This
interruption raised concerns that reduced natural immune boosting, combined with the already known rapid
waning of aP-induced immunity, could exacerbate pertussis resurgence once restrictions were lifted. The
manuscript correctly identifies this epidemiological and immunological interplay as the central concerns.
The authors address this issue by leveraging a nationwide prospective serosurveillance cohort to monitor
antibody dynamics and infection incidence across age groups. Their data provide evidence that waning
population immunity left certain groups (notably children and adolescents) more susceptible, which
contributed to the sharp increase in cases from 2023 onwards. However, while the cohort design is robust and
the longitudinal sampling a strength, the study is limited in its ability to fully disentangle the interplay between
vaccination history, natural boosting, and other epidemiological drivers (e.g., bacterial adaptation, changes in
diagnostic practices, or underdiagnosis).
Response:
Thank you for your constructive feedback. We agree that disentangling the complex interplay between the
various factors is important, and do acknowledge that our study does not, and cannot fully separate this
complex interplay. This would require a prospective study design that follows the same individuals from the
infant immunization schedule all the way into adolescence to generate a complete history of vaccination and
exposures to the bacterium, paired with tracking the bacteria circulating during that study period and
performing molecular typing of all infections. Our study was restricted to antibody response data only, limited
to infection data from current reporting systems, which we addressed in our discussion.
However, the serosurveillance approach allows the detection of pertussis infections not driven by clinical
criteria nor by clinical reporting systems, which is anticipated to identify a much higher B. pertussis infection
prevalency, mainly among those where B. pertussis infections have low clinical impact. This is indeed what we
demonstrated among the different age groups. In our study, we detected a higher percentage of the population
to be infected with B. pertussis during the peak in notifications. This suggest much higher circulation of B.
pertussis compared to that of the clinical notifications, which we highlighted in our discussion with the
following sentence:
Line 331-337: The increased number of infections in the 6-18 year age group was also evident in the notification data of
syndromic cases in the Netherlands and other countries (2, 3, 25). However, according to our serological criteria of infection,
we detected a much higher infection rate (35.4%) compared to the number of notifications in the 6-18 years age group
(0.24%). This difference is likely caused by the high prevalence of mild and asymptomatic infections not leading to seeking
medical care, against a relative low clinical manifestation of B. pertussis infections within this age group in general (5, 12,
26).
Despite the use of serological tools, we were able to detect vaccination event based on combined anti-Ptx and
anti-Ttx IgG boosts, as described in the previous comment. The reviewer is correct that we have do not have
vaccination records on individual basis. Population-wide the vaccination coverage is slightly decreasing. To
clarify this to the reader, a sentence in the introduction regarding vaccination coverage based on the Dutch
vaccination coverage report was added:
Line 53-59: Of special concern is the decrease in vaccination coverage in the Netherlands that has been observed over the
past years, with 92.2% of the infants born in 2019 who have been fully vaccinated by the age of two (8). Since 2019, the
maternal Diphtheria-Tetanus-acellular Pertussis (Tdap) vaccination is implemented in the Dutch NIP to increase the level of
maternally-derived immunological protection in the first months post birth (2). However, this is not implemented globally
and pertussis remains one of the least controlled vaccine preventable diseases.
Bacterial adaptation is an important factor in the increased incidence of pertussis infections, especially in
combination with new vaccine schedules. We know that after the COVID-19 pandemic, fewer pertactin
deficient pertussis strain were circulating compared to the years before COVID-19 (9). We were not able to
include this in in our study due to the nature of our study, but we have added a paragraph to the discussion to
address this point:
Line 366-374: These findings show the need of improved pertussis vaccines that induce local antibodies and T-cell
responses. This is essential for prevention of colonization and clearance of B. pertussis and improve the control of pertussis
circulation. It is known that there is continuous adaptation of B. pertussis to its host (35). Since the introduction of the aP
vaccine, an increase of Prn-deficient strains has been observed in many countries (36). However, typing of Dutch pertussis
isolates in 2023 and 2024 showed less circulation of Prn-deficient pertussis strains, which we think could be related to the
decline in immunity reported in our study (37). This ongoing bacterial adaptation is an additional challenge to long-term
pertussis control and also shows the need for continued B. pertussis molecular surveillance, in addition to monitoring of
immunity in the population.
Another limitation is the heavy reliance on serological markers (IgG, IgA against Ptx, FHA, and Prn) as analogs of
immunity or to propose protection surrogates. While informative, antibody concentrations alone may not fully
capture protective immunity, especially given the growing recognition of the role of cellular responses in
pertussis control. The authors acknowledge waning immunity but could have more critically contextualized
their findings within the broader debate over the adequacy of current pertussis vaccination strategies.
In summary, the manuscript provides valuable national data on pertussis resurgence after the COVID-19
pandemic and highlights waning vaccine-induced immunity as a major driver. Yet, its framing could be
strengthened by situating the findings within the broader global context of pertussis resurgence, addressing
alternative explanations beyond antibody waning, and more explicitly discussing implications for vaccination
policy.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

After relative absence of Bordetella pertussis during the COVID-19 pandemic, notifications in the Netherlands were increased from May 2023 till September 2024. We monitored the largest pertussis outbreak in decades and investigated underlying immunological dynamics based on IgG and IgA antibodies against pertussis antigens (Ptx, FHA & Prn). We analyzed serum from 418 participants (2–87 years) at five time points (November 2022-October 2024) from a nationwide prospective serosurveillance study (PIENTER-Corona). Weighted incidence over two years was 6.3% (95% CI: 4.4-8.2) in the Dutch population, and 35% (95% CI: 26.2-44.6) in 6-18 y-olds. Children aged 6-12 years, who received a booster vaccination at 4 years, showed lowest anti-Ptx IgG concentrations after the period of reduced circulation. Infected individuals had lower pre-infection anti-FHA IgG and IgA concentrations than matched uninfected individuals. Prolonged coughing was reported by 16% of the infected individuals. Our findings highlight the B. pertussis outbreak was preceded by waning immunity, particularly after acellular pertussis booster vaccination. The small proportion of symptomatic infections implies sufficient protection by the vaccine against disease but not transmission.

---

## Introduction

During the COVID-19 pandemic, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), including wearing face masks, social distancing, closure of schools and working from home, were introduced to limit the circulation of SARS-CoV-2. This not only led to a reduction of SARS-CoV-2 notifications but also to a decrease of notifications of other airborne-transmissible pathogens, including pertussis, or whooping cough, a disease caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis (Fig. 1)1–3. Notably, this reduction of pertussis notifications likely reflects reduced circulation of the bacterium, which lasted for almost 3 years. Since May 2023, pertussis notifications rose, cumulating in the largest pertussis outbreak to date since 2012 in the Netherlands (Fig. 1)2. This trend has been observed in multiple Europe countries2,3.

Pertussis is a highly contagious respiratory infection. During the catarrhal stage, symptoms mostly resemble those of a common cold. In the paroxysmal phase, which is the most symptomatic stage, symptoms are often coughing, inspiratory whooping and post-tussive vomiting4. Infections can occur at any age but can cause serious disease in (predominantly unvaccinated) infants and older adults4. Vaccinated individuals are more likely to have an atypical, mild, or even asymptomatic infection5. Since the use of the whole cell pertussis (wP) vaccine—containing inactivated bacteria—in the Dutch national immunization program (NIP) in 1957, a drop in the incidence of pertussis was recorded6. Despite vaccination, re-emergence was apparent as of 1996, with incidence peaking every 3–5 years7. In 2001, an acellular pertussis (aP) booster vaccination, containing inactivated pertussis toxin (Ptx), filamentous hemagglutinin (FHA), pertactin (Prn) and sometimes fimbriae 2/3 (Fim 2/3), was implemented at 4 years of age2. In 2005, the wP vaccine for the primary series was also replaced by an aP vaccine due to high reactogenicity of the wP vaccine2. Despite these changes, pertussis incidence remained high and a threat for infants too young to be vaccinated2. Of special concern is the decrease in vaccination coverage in the Netherlands that has been observed over the past years. The WHO and RIVM reported that the percentage of fully vaccinated infants by the age of two declined from 96 to 97% in the 2010 birth cohort to 92–94% in the 2019 birth cohort and 89–93% in the 2022 birth cohort8,9. Since 2019, the maternal diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccination is implemented in the Dutch NIP to increase the level of maternally-derived immunological protection in the first months post birth2. However, this is not implemented globally, and pertussis remains one of the least controlled vaccine-preventable diseases.

As B. pertussis generally circulates continuously, leading to notifications year-round, there is no clear understanding of what drives the epidemiology and the elevation of notifications every 3–5 years. Notably, while respiratory syncytial virus and seasonal coronaviruses re-appeared rapidly when most NPIs for COVID-19 were lifted mid-2022, pertussis notifications increased nearly a year later (Fig. 1). The period of reduced B. pertussis circulation provided a unique opportunity to monitor waning immunity against B. pertussis and how changes in immunity may have affected the rapid increase of notifications from 2023 onwards. We use a Dutch nationwide prospective cohort (2–87 year of age), setup since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, to investigate the age-specific incidence of B. pertussis infections between November 2022 and October 2024. We identify an overall 6.4% incidence, and an incidence of 35.4% in children aged 6–18 years during this two-year period, which is caused by the combined effect of waning vaccine immunity and a prolonged period of reduced pertussis circulation.

---

## Results

Study population
The participants for this study were part of the PICO cohort and resided across the country (Supplementary Fig. 1A). Slightly more women were included compared to men (Table 1). Vaccination coverage in children based on long-term protection anti-Ttx IgG (>0.1 IU/ml) was estimated to be 98.9% at baseline (i.e., November 2022). Overall, anti-Ttx IgG antibodies were detected in 95.2% of the included participants.

Overall anti-Ptx IgG concentrations by age were determined at the start and end of the study (Fig. 2A). At the start, lower concentrations were observed in 6–12-year-old individuals as compared to 2–5-year-olds and adults (p < 0.005). Anti-Ptx IgG concentrations of 6–12-year-old individuals had increased in October 2024 as compared to those at the start of the study (p < 0.001), despite large variation (Fig. 2B). In all other age groups, no significantly different concentrations were observed between both sampling rounds (Fig. 2B).

Pertussis infections during the study period
Antibody rises attributed to DTaP or Tdap vaccination during the study period were observed in the 2–5 years age group (13 cases) and in the 19–39 years age group (4 cases) (Fig. 3A, blue lines). The weighted incidence of B. pertussis infections in the general Dutch population—based on the serological criteria in the current study—was 0.6% between November 2022 and April 2023, 1.4% between April and November 2023, 3.5% between November 2023 and April 2024, and 1.5% between April and October 2024 (Table 1 and Fig. 3A, orange lines). The weighted cumulative incidence in the Dutch population (2–87 years) during this two-year period was estimated at 6.3%. The highest incidence (35.4%) was found among the age group 6–18 years (Fig. 3B and Table 1). The increase in anti-Ptx IgG concentrations after infection was also paralleled by an increase in anti-FHA and anti-Prn IgG and IgA and anti-Ptx IgA concentrations (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Individuals with serological evidence of B. pertussis infection did not report increased symptoms compared to uninfected individuals. Prolonged coughing (>2 weeks) during the past year was reported by 16% of the infected individuals between 6 and 18 years (5/32) in the last sampling round, of whom two contacted the GP. No significant difference was observed concerning prolonged coughing in uninfected individuals (22/75 (29.3%); p = 0.21).

Because the higher pertussis incidence according to serological detections, including age group differences (Table 1), and the syndromic notifications (Supplementary Fig. 1B), the serological infection prevalence based on anti-Ptx IgG categories was further estimated in an additional subset in October 2024. The additional cross-sectional subset showed a similar proportion of individuals with no indication of recent infection (<50 IU/mL) in the 6–18, 19–39, and 60+ year age groups compared to the longitudinal cohort (Supplementary Fig. 4). The 40–59 years age group indicated a lower proportion of recently infected individuals in the longitudinal serosurvey in October 2024 compared to the cross-sectional study (p = 0.0028) (Supplementary Fig. 4).

The cross-sectional subset from October 2024 was also compared with previous cross-sectional serosurveys conducted using similar methodologies7. All age groups show a similar proportion of individuals with no indication of recent infection compared to the Pienter-2 study (2006–2007) and the Pienter-3 study (2016–2017) except for individuals in the 40–59 years age group (Fig. 4). The additional subset from October 2024 showed a higher proportion of individuals without indication of recent infection compared to the Pienter-3 study (p = 0.045).

To address whether the lower anti-Ptx IgG concentrations within the 6–18 years age group in November 2022 (Fig. 2) might be related to a more rapid antibody waning after (primary series or booster) vaccination, a linear mixed-effects model was applied in individuals who remained uninfected or up the point of infection and unvaccinated. The 2–5 year-olds showed the highest anti-Ptx IgG concentrations at the start of the study (16.45 IU/mL; p < 0.05 compared to other age groups). The 6–12 years age group displayed lower antibody concentrations at the start of the study period compared to adults (5.83 IU/mL vs. 7.28 IU/mL; p = 0.009). The fastest antibody decay was observed in the 2–5 years age group with the duration of antibody decay to 50% of 17.8 months (Fig. 5; p < 0.001 for the slope). Antibody decay was also noticed in the 6–12, 13–18 and ≥19 years age group (p < 0.001 for the slopes). The duration of antibody decay to 50% in the 6–12, 13–18, and ≥19 years age group was 48.5, 102.5 and 84.1 months, respectively.

Anti-Ptx, FHA and Prn concentrations in individuals 6–18 years
Anti-FHA IgG concentrations of infected individuals between 6 and 18 years of age appeared significantly lower prior to infection compared to age-matched uninfected individuals (13.4 IU/mL (95% CI 9.8–18.2) vs. 27.9 IU/mL (95% CI 22.1–35.1); p = 0.002), as well as anti-FHA IgA concentrations (1.0 IU/mL (95% CI 0.8–1.4) vs. 2.1 IU/mL (95% CI 1.6-2.8); p = 0.006) (Fig. 6B, E). Comparison of anti-Ptx, anti-Prn IgG, and IgA concentrations revealed no statistically significant differences, nor did the control antigen rubella IgG concentrations.

Using the Youden index, protective cut-off values for anti-FHA IgG and IgA were estimated. This resulted in cutoffs of 13.6 and 1.6 IU/mL for IgG and IgA respectively, with corresponding AUC values of 0.74 and 0.72 (specificity of 78% and 63% and sensitivity of 71% and 74%, respectively) (Supplementary Fig. 5). We found no conclusive evidence that individuals who reporting (prolonged) cough symptoms had statistically significant lower anti-Ptx IgG and IgA concentrations, although the numbers were low (p = 0.084 and p = 0.051, respectively).

## Methods

Study population
The PIENTER-corona (PICO) study was setup at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic to study immunity to SARS-CoV-2 across the Dutch population with repeated sampling of the same individuals (~10,000 unique participants) until the end of 2024 (in total 13 study rounds), as described previously37,40,41. The PICO-study protocol was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee MEC-U, the Netherlands (Clinical Trial Registration NTR8473), and conformed to the principles embodied in the Declaration of Helsinki. Informed consent was obtained from all adult participants and from parents or legal guardians of minors prior to participation.

Here, we randomly selected an age-stratified subset with completed questionnaires and samples (n = 419) from study rounds 9–13 (November 2022–October 2024) (age range: 2–87 years). Because of the vaccination schedule and expected incidence in children, smaller age windows were used (Table 1). For the overall analysis, we expected a 6% incidence rate7 and aimed for a one-sided precision of 2.5%, resulting in a minimum required sample size of 347 individuals (α = 0.05, power = 80%). Taking into account a potential loss of 15% of follow-up samples, at least 408 participants were needed in the longitudinal analysis. For all age groups, we were able to include sufficient individuals, except for the youngest age group (2–5 years), where only 43 individuals were available, who were all included.

To investigate changes in antibody concentrations, samples were collected in November 2022 (median inclusion date: 8 November), April 2023 (median: 25 April), and November 2023 (median: 6 November) (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Sampling volumes were adequate for all but one participant, and serum samples from one participant had to be excluded due to technical issues, so serum samples from 418 participants could be tested. Since the pertussis notifications were still elevated after November 2023, follow-up samples collected in April 2024 (median: 15 April; 382 participants (91%)) and October 2024 (median: 14 October; 358 participants (85%)) were included as well.

Participants sent in a fingerstick blood sample in a microtainer by mail. Serum obtained from these blood samples was stored at −20°C awaiting analyses. The participants completed a questionnaire during each sampling round, including, amongst others, questions about sociodemographic characteristics, COVID-19-related symptoms (general, respiratory, and gastrointestinal) in the past months and behavioral factors. Each round, participants were requested to report respiratory symptoms, including cough, sore throat and runny nose and fever, which are associated with B. pertussis infection24. In the final sampling round, a specific question about prolonged coughing (>2 weeks) in the past year was added.

Detection of antibodies
Serum samples were tested for anti-Ptx, anti-tetanus toxin (Ttx; to control for vaccination) and anti-rubella (as an independent control to monitor antibody variation) IgG antibodies at all sampling rounds using an in-house validated fluorescent bead-based multiplex immunoassay as described before42,43. During the last three sampling rounds, most infections were detected, hence, these samples were tested additionally for anti-FHA and anti-Prn IgG and IgA and Ptx IgA (see Supplementary Methods for further details on the assay).

Criteria for pertussis infection
Active or recent infection with B. pertussis was detected by an increase in Ptx-specific antibodies44. Diagnostic confirmation of recent pertussis infection in paired samples, with the second sample at 2–4 weeks interval, normally uses a >3-fold increase in anti-Ptx IgG concentration with a final concentration >20 IU/mL44–46. Here, we used a ≥2-fold increase criterion due to a longer time interval between two measurements. We expected more waning of antibodies within that period, consequently leading to a lower fold-change between consecutive samples. For participants of whom a sample was missing in November 2022 (n = 1) or April 2024 (n = 11), an infection could be ruled out as they remained below the cutoff in the subsequent round (April 2023 or October 2024).

Part of the participants in this study could have elevated anti-Ptx concentrations due to DTaP or Tdap infant, booster or maternal vaccination (Table 2). For children <5 years of age and women who reported to be pregnant, a ≥2-fold increase in anti-Ptx IgG and anti-Ttx IgG concentrations with anti-Ptx IgG concentrations >5 IU/mL indicated a recent (maternal) vaccination. Because the Tdap booster vaccination contains reduced concentrations of the pertussis components, and vaccination induces a weaker antibody response compared to natural infection, a lower anti-Ptx IgG cutoff was used not to miss vaccination events47. The validity of this approach was tested on sera from individuals seeking medical care with confirmed pertussis infection (see Supplementary Methods).

In addition, a (cross-sectional) estimation of infection prevalence was conducted with an additional sample from the last PICO round (October 2024, n = 761) and compared with the longitudinal data from November 2022 and October 2024 and two cross-sectional serosurveys that were carried out in the past using the same measurements (Pienter-2, 2006/2007 and Pienter-3, 2016/2017)7,48. As the earlier surveys did not include sequential sampling, the definition used in our analysis so far could not be used for this comparison. As applied previously, we used anti-Ptx IgG concentrations of ≥100 IU/mL as the most stringent diagnostic criterium associated with a recent infection in the past 6 months44, concentrations between 50 and 100 IU/mL for an infection in the past 6–12 months, and those under 50 IU/mL for a less recent infection7,49.

Statistical analyses
Data cleaning and statistical analyses were performed using Rstudio (R version 4.4.0, R Core Team, Vienna, Austria) using packages nlme50, MatchIt51, effects52 and pROC53 and SAS v.9.4. (SAS Institute Inc., USA). For all analyses, age at the moment of inclusion (November 2022) was used, unless specified otherwise. The antibody data were log-transformed, and Loess (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing) curves were generated to visualize antibody concentrations across all ages at the start and end point of the study. A two-sided paired t-test on log-transformed data was used to compare the anti-Ptx IgG concentrations at the start and end point of the study for different age groups. An two-sided unpaired t-test on log-transformed data was used to compare the anti-Ptx IgG concentrations at the start of the study period between age groups.

Pertussis incidence per study round, cumulative incidence across the study period and seroprevalence estimated (with 95% confidence intervals (CI)) were calculated taking into account the survey design (with regions as strata and municipalities as clusters, where applicable), and weighted on age, sex, ethnic background and degree of urbanization following census data from the statistics Netherlands of the respected periods to match the general Dutch population, as described previously40. Estimates were provided for the overall population and by age group. For the pertussis incidence per study round, age during the specific round was used. Differences in seroprevalence between groups were assessed by estimating the parameters of the beta distribution using the method of moments. Risk ratios and their 95% Cis and two-sided p-values were calculated based on Monte Carlo simulations, and reported where applicable.

Waning of anti-Ptx IgG concentrations per age group was evaluated in individuals who remained uninfected (or up the point of infection) and unvaccinated with a linear mixed-effects model on log-transformed values, using the nlme package. The model contained random intercepts and slopes per age group, and the fixed effect was constructed as the interaction of time and age. The results are expressed as the predicted geometric mean concentrations of anti-Ptx IgG per age group and PICO study round with corresponding 95% CIs.

Pre-infection IgG and IgA antibody concentrations against B. pertussis antigens implicated in host colonization (FHA and Prn) were compared between participants with a confirmed infection (n = 38) and uninfected controls (n = 68) matched by age and sampling round. Antibodies to the independent antigen rubella served as control to monitor antibody variations. Log-transformed IgG concentrations were compared with a t-test and IgA concentrations with a Mann–Whitney U test due to not normally distributed data. Finally, to approximate the sensitivity and specificity of a potential correlate of protection, the Youden index of the receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curve analysis were used.

More detailed feedback and comments.
The manuscript addresses an important and timely issue: the resurgence of Bordetella pertussis in the post–COVID-19 era. Pertussis remains the least controlled vaccine-preventable disease, and its re-emergence is a global concern. Countries that transitioned from whole-cell (wP) to acellular pertussis (aP) vaccines have consistently reported shorter-lived immunity, increased susceptibility in adolescents and adults, and recurrent epidemics every 3–5 years. The COVID-19 pandemic, with its widespread non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), provided an unusual natural experiment by temporarily interrupting pathogen circulation. This interruption raised concerns that reduced natural immune boosting, combined with the already known rapid waning of aP-induced immunity, could exacerbate pertussis resurgence once restrictions were lifted. The manuscript correctly identifies this epidemiological and immunological interplay as the central concerns.
The authors address this issue by leveraging a nationwide prospective serosurveillance cohort to monitor antibody dynamics and infection incidence across age groups. Their data provide evidence that waning population immunity left certain groups (notably children and adolescents) more susceptible, which contributed to the sharp increase in cases from 2023 onwards. However, while the cohort design is robust and the longitudinal sampling a strength, the study is limited in its ability to fully disentangle the interplay between vaccination history, natural boosting, and other epidemiological drivers (e.g., bacterial adaptation, changes in diagnostic practices, or underdiagnosis).
Another limitation is the heavy reliance on serological markers (IgG, IgA against Ptx, FHA, and Prn) as analogs of immunity or to propose protection surrogates. While informative, antibody concentrations alone may not fully capture protective immunity, especially given the growing recognition of the role of cellular responses in pertussis control. The authors acknowledge waning immunity but could have more critically contextualized their findings within the broader debate over the adequacy of current pertussis vaccination strategies.
In summary, the manuscript provides valuable national data on pertussis resurgence after the COVID-19 pandemic and highlights waning vaccine-induced immunity as a major driver. Yet, its framing could be strengthened by situating the findings within the broader global context of pertussis resurgence, addressing alternative explanations beyond antibody waning, and more explicitly discussing implications for vaccination policy.
